nameStory: The 'Tellin Semele' gets its name from a case of mistaken identity that stuck around! Early naturalists thought this small clam was related to the tellin clams (which have thin, delicate shells), but it's actually in the semele family. The scientific name Cumingia honors British naturalist Hugh Cuming, a 19th-century shell collector who sailed the world gathering specimens.
description: The Tellin Semele is a small, burrowing clam with a distinctly wavy or zigzag-patterned shell that looks like someone drew squiggly lines across it. This little mollusk typically grows to about half an inch to three-quarters of an inch long, making it easy to overlook among beach debris. Its two-part shell (called a bivalve) is relatively thick for its size and usually whitish to pale yellow. Like other clams, it lives buried in sand or mud and feeds by filtering tiny particles from the water.

idTips.label: Zigzag Shell Pattern
idTips.description: Look for distinctive wavy, zigzag lines running across the shell surface - these irregular ridges feel slightly raised when you run your finger over them and create a unique fingerprint-like pattern

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: The shell is roughly triangular or wedge-shaped when viewed from the side, with a rounded front end and more pointed back end that feels sturdy and thick for such a small clam

idTips.label: Size Range
idTips.description: Typically measures 12-20mm (about half to three-quarters of an inch) long - roughly the size of your thumbnail or a large pea

idTips.label: Color and Texture
idTips.description: Fresh shells are whitish to pale yellow with a slightly chalky texture, while beached specimens may be bleached pure white or stained brown from sediments

idTips.label: Shell Thickness
idTips.description: Despite its small size, the shell feels surprisingly solid and thick when held - much sturdier than the paper-thin shells of true tellins

habitat: Look for Tellin Semeles in sandy and muddy bottoms of shallow coastal waters, typically in protected bays, estuaries, and tidal flats along New England's coast. They prefer areas with moderate wave action and are often found buried 2-4 inches deep in sediment where they can filter-feed from the water column. You're most likely to find their empty shells washed up on sandy beaches after storms, especially in areas near salt marshes and eelgrass beds.

seasonality.spring: Fresh shells may wash ashore after winter storms, often mixed with other small clam shells in wrack lines. This is a good time to search for specimens as spring tides expose more beach area.
seasonality.summer: Peak time for finding shells on beaches as increased boat traffic and summer storms stir up bottom sediments. Living clams are actively feeding in shallow waters but remain buried and hard to spot.
seasonality.fall: Autumn storms frequently wash shells ashore, and this is often the best season for beachcombing. Look for shells mixed in with seaweed and other debris after nor'easters.
seasonality.winter: Shells continue to wash up during winter storms, though beachcombing conditions may be harsh. Winter specimens are often well-cleaned by wave action, making the zigzag pattern easier to see.

funFact: Despite being called a 'Tellin Semele,' this little clam can actually jump! When disturbed, it can use its muscular foot to flip itself through the water - a surprising escape mechanism for what most people think of as a sedentary shellfish.
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with small tellin clams, but remember the texture trick: Tellin Semeles feel thick and sturdy like a tiny dinner plate, while true tellins are paper-thin and fragile. The zigzag pattern is your best friend - true tellins have smooth shells or simple concentric rings, never those distinctive wavy ridges.
contextualKnowledge: The name confusion between 'tellin' and 'semele' reflects how challenging it can be to classify small clams - even scientists got it wrong initially! This highlights how shell collecting and identification improved over time as more specimens were studied and compared.
compareHints: Since this is the only Cumingia species in New England waters, compare it with other small clams in the region. Unlike soft-shell clams which have thin, easily-broken shells, or hard clams which are much larger and rounder, the Tellin Semele's combination of small size, thick shell, and distinctive zigzag ridges makes it unique among New England bivalves.
